content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a federated causal discovery which aims to learn causal graphs from multiple observational datasets that are stored locally and cannot be shared due to privacy concern.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

•	First paper to consider causal discovery under federated learning setting. 

•	The method allows local datasets to be non-iid, which is likely in practice. 

Weaknesses:

•	Empirical results can be improved by 

      o	Including more competing methods beyond continuous optimization approaches. The PC and GES algorithms are non-identifiable. Many identifiable alternative approaches exist such as ANM. 

      o	Considering more real data validations. Currently, only one real data result is presented. And that dataset is not in the federated setting. To show the real usage of the proposed method, at least one real distributed dataset is needed in my opinion. 

      o	Simulations show the proposed method is superior when data are generated under the proposed model. It will be more interesting to see how the model performs under model misspecification.

•	Hyperparameter tuning and sensitivity analysis. Since causal structural learning can be seen as an unsupervised learning task, tuning hyperparameter is particularly important. From Section A.5, it looks like some hyperparameters are fixed to certain values and others are tuned by simulations. For the former, I believe a sensitivity analysis is in order. For the latter, how does this strategy generalize to real data or simulation settings that are substantially different from the scenarios used for tuning? In fact, it is not clear to me what the authors meant by “tune these two parameters via the same scale of experiment with seeds 1 ∼ 10”. Can the authors provide more details on that?

5. **In fact, it is not clear to me what the authors meant by “tune these two parameters via the same scale of experiment with seeds 1 ∼ 10”. Can the authors provide more details on that?**  
   Notice that all reported results of simulated experiments in our paper are tested with seeds $2021\sim 2030$, while the hyperparameters are searched with seeds $1\sim 10$. This implementation is to simulate the training datasets and testing datasets. In simulated experiments, we first randomly generate a DAG and then the causal mechanisms by randomly selecting linear or non-linear functions. Then, observations are sampled according to our ANM model. That is to say, the random seed decides all the aforementioned things, including causal graph and dataset. We use seeds $1 \sim 10$ to simulate the training sets, and all hyperparameters are tuned on these datasets. Then, these selected hyper-parameters are applied to datasets generated by other seeds for testing the performance of our methods. You can find similar implementation in MCSL (Appendix G.1)[1].  

Based on the aforementioned discussions, we hope that your doubts can be well eliminated. Please feel free to let us know if you still have any further concerns.

4. **Hyperparameter tuning and sensitivity analysis. Since causal structural learning can be seen as an unsupervised learning task, tuning hyperparameter is particularly important. From Section A.5, it looks like some hyperparameters are fixed to certain values and others are tuned by simulations. For the former, I believe a sensitivity analysis is in order. For the latter, how does this strategy generalize to real data or simulation settings that are substantially different from the scenarios used for tuning?**  
   Very nice suggestion! Following your kind suggestion, we would divide our parameters into two classes. The first class would affect the model selection, including $\alpha$, $\rho$, $it_{fl}$ and $\lambda_{l_1}$. The second class would affect the optimization procedures, which basically are some max-iterations limitation parameters.  
   - ***For the former, I believe a sensitivity analysis is in order.***  
      Here, we add the sensitivity analysis experiments for three hyper-parameters including $\alpha_{init}$, $it_{fl}$ and $\lambda_{l_1}$. The numerical results are as followings:  
      Table 4: Sensitive analysis of $it_{fl}$ (Non-IID, 20 nodes, ER2).  
      |$it_{fl}$| 10         | 20         | 50         | 100        | 250        | 500         |
      |-----|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|-------------|
      | SHD | 7.40 $\pm$ 6.07 | 6.50 $\pm$ 4.34 | 6.60 $\pm$ 4.13 | 6.30 $\pm$ 5.00 | 6.80 $\pm$ 5.93 | **6.20 $\pm$ 4.51**  |
      | TPR | 0.89 $\pm$ 0.10 | **0.90 $\pm$ 0.08** | 0.90 $\pm$ 0.09 | 0.90 $\pm$ 0.09 | 0.90 $\pm$ 0.10 | 0.90 $\pm$ 0.09  |

      From the above experimental results, we find that our method is relatively robust to $it_{fl}$.  

      Table 5: Sensitive analysis of $\lambda_{l_1}$ (Non-IID, 20 nodes, ER2). 
      |$\lambda_{l_1}$| 0          | 0.01       | 0.1        | 1           | 10          | 100          |
      |-----|------------|------------|------------|-------------|-------------|--------------|
      | SHD | 6.40 $\pm$ 4.88 | **5.70 $\pm$ 4.05** | 7.00 $\pm$ 5.23 | 11.10 $\pm$ 6.07 | 28.70 $\pm$ 5.04 | 35.30 $\pm$ 5.37  |
      | TPR | 0.90 $\pm$ 0.08 | **0.91 $\pm$ 0.07** | 0.88 $\pm$ 0.10 | 0.72 $\pm$ 0.13  | 0.22 $\pm$ 0.09  | 0.02 $\pm$ 0.03   |

      $\lambda_{l_1}$ is the coefficient of $l_1$ sparsity, which will affect the final results. Because we have no sparsity information of the underlying causal graph, we set $\lambda_{l_1}=0.01$ in all settings. When dealing with real data, we recommend the audiences to adjust this parameter by using our parameter-tuning method provided in the Appendix.

      Table 6: Sensitive analysis of $\alpha_{init}$ (Non-IID, 20 nodes, ER2).

      |$\alpha_{init}$| 0.5         | 0.1        | 0.05       | 0.01       | 0.005       | 0.001       |
      |-----|-------------|------------|------------|------------|-------------|-------------|
      | SHD | 26.10 $\pm$ 5.49 | 8.50 $\pm$ 6.00 | 6.30 $\pm$ 5.12 | 5.90 $\pm$ 4.78 | **5.60 $\pm$ 5.06**  | 6.10 $\pm$ 4.30  |
      | TPR | 0.28 $\pm$ 0.12  | 0.80 $\pm$ 0.13 | 0.87 $\pm$ 0.11 | 0.89 $\pm$ 0.10 | **0.92 $\pm$ 0.08** | 0.91 $\pm$ 0.08  |

      These results are exactly as expected. As discussed in our paper, our method tries to maximize the likelihood term of the total loss in the early stages, which is important to find the final ground-truth DAG. If you put a relatively large $\alpha_{init}$, the early learning stages would be affected. Therefore, we recommend directly taking $0$ as $\alpha_{init}$. 

   - ***For the latter, how does this strategy generalize to real data or simulation settings that are substantially different from the scenarios used for tuning?***  
   As illustrated in our paper, the hyper-parameters choices of $\rho_{init}$ and $\beta$ of DS-FCD need to be tuned according to the scale of variables. If you have real data at hand, these two hyper-parameters can be firstly searched on some simulated data of the same variable scale. Then these two searched parameters can be directly applied to the real data. We also find that the sparsity parameter $\lambda_{l_1}$ is also important for the performance of our method on real data. In our paper, we have in detail described how to tune $\lambda_{l_1}$ on the real data. Of course, you can also fine-tune $\rho_{init}$ and $\beta$ in the same way.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors introduce a federated learning method for causal discovery in which each client tries to learn the DAG and neural networks to approximate the SEM. The SCM, and associated DAG, of participating clients are aggregated and processed by the server and then sent to each client for updating their personalized model.
content.main_review:
# Abstract

You claim " However, data owners gradually refuse to share personalized data to avoid privacy leakage, making this task more troublesome by cutting off the first step" - is this really true? I have not heard this before and it seems data is becoming easier and easier to access as it becomes the norm, certainly within research, to open-source data. Hence, can you point to some sources? I find one in the body of your paper. It seems to be a rather weak case for developing a whole new method.

# Introduction

- Typo: "randomized controlled trials" -> randomized control trials

- Isn't CSL simply CD i.e. causal discovery?

- Typo: "owning to the issue of" -> owing to the issue of

- "data owners gradually prefer not to share their personalized data with others" this is a major claim for which you provide one source. Please dig into this in a lot more detail because it goes against what is commonly perceived. Certainly, privacy has become a much bigger issue but that is dealt with through anonymization not (as far as I know at least) blank refusal to share the data.

- Style: perhaps stick with either underlining text of emphasising it through italics; having both is a bit too much.

- Figure 1: you haven't told us yet what SHDs stands for so you may want to spell that out in the figure legend otherwise we'll have to search for it in the main body.

- How reasonable is your first assumption? That seems like a very big ask of the data and not mild at all. SEMs and the DAG usually go hand in hand, perhaps the noise model may change a bit between datasets but not the mechanisms themselves (but again, examples would be very welcome). 

- Isn't the, what you call "CGL" (I think you mean the learned graph), part very revealing w.r.t. privacy? You may not have access to each individual but instead you are providing organisations with causal information as to how a group of people causally act. In the wrong hands that could be very dangerous. Please comment.

# Preliminaries

- You ought to reference Pearl's Causality (2000) and specifically page 203 which defines structural causal models and the associated causal graphical model (which you for some reason decide to call a graphical causal model which is not standard).
- You do not mention non-manipulative variables in $X$ nor do you mention the exogenous set $U$ nor confounders - are these not relevant for you method?
- You may want to tell us what the assumptions say rather than just referencing them. You may have have a novice audience who study causality for the first time reading your paper.

# Problem definition

- I would recommend a nomenclature for your symbols
- What is $k$?
- You are using notation $\{[m]\}$ - what does that mean? Is it short for $0:m$ or however you're indexing the first item.

# Methodology

- You'll need to spend a lot more time on figure 2. It is not self-contained at all. You are introducing notation in the figure before you've introduced in the paper. What does each dashed box mean? What are the layers on the top? Why are there arrows? What do the arrows mean? You say you share DAG ok, but then the first box has a matrix which is different from the other two.
- Section 4.1 is preliminaries no? Why have you placed it under the method section?
- Sentence construction: "preventing the efficient of penalty" what does that mean?
- Sentence construction: "identifying up the ground-truth"

## Privacy and cost discussion

- This section is the most important. It should be at the top of the paper. This it the main motivation for the method. You are saying that you avoid personalised data leakage because you are _only_ sharing the causal graph. You are sharing $\mathbf{U}^{c_k}$ which you say is the same for all clients (but still index it for each client) but then you claim that because the ANM may be different and the SEM may be different too, you are in fact not _actually_ sharing any personal data. Never mind that those assumptions are questionable the fact that you are sharing the DAG alone should be cause for concern (and even that assumption is also very questionable - that all clients have observations generated from the same DAG).

    Nice suggestion! In our early version, we did put this part in the Section of preliminaries because these methods are not proposed by us and are some general knowledge. We put this content in our method part by considering that the acyclicity constraint formulation is tightly associated with our whole method. All the references are well-cited to show their credits.  
    According to your suggestion, we rethink this thing and feel like that this part should be put in the Section of Preliminaries. We will update this change in our revision. 
18. **Sentence construction: "preventing the efficient of penalty" what does that mean?**  
    Thanks. This is a typo of "coefficient" by "efficient". 
19. **Sentence construction: "identifying up the ground-truth"**  
    We have changed this sentence to "In general, unique identification of the ground truth DAG is impossible from purely observational data without some specific assumptions."
## Privacy and cost discussion
20. **This section is the most important. It should be at the top of the paper. This it the main motivation for the method. You are saying that you avoid personalised data leakage because you are only sharing the causal graph. You are sharing $\bf U^{c_k}$ which you say is the same for all clients (but still index it for each client) but then you claim that because the ANM may be different and the SEM may be different too, you are in fact not actually sharing any personal data. Never mind that those assumptions are questionable the fact that you are sharing the DAG alone should be cause for concern (and even that assumption is also very questionable - that all clients have observations generated from the same DAG).**  
   We briefly conclude your considerations into 3 sub-problems.  
   (1). ***This section should be at the top of the paper.***  
   We agree that "privacy protection" is one of the main motivations of our method. We will emphasize our motivation in the previous part. In our view, we think that these discussions are of the post-method things because this is highly related to our method but not the topic. Therefore, we still prefer to leave this part unchanged.  
   (2). ***You are sharing $\bf U^{c_k}$ which you say is the same for all clients (but still index it for each client).***  
   As explained above, the ground-truth causal graph is assumed to be the same. However, during the learning procedures, $U$ of different clients may not be the same at every second. That is the reason that we index it.  
   (3). ***You claim that because the ANM may be different and the SEM may be different too, you are in fact not actually sharing any personal data.***  
   Yes, in the Non-IID setting, we assume that ANMs are different among clients. Considering the sharing the personal data things, we have narrowed our "privacy leakage" expression to "raw data leakage". As explained, we assume that DAG is shared among all clients.     Sorry for this. $[m]$ is taken for $\{1,2,\cdots,m\}$, which is fixed to start from $1$. This explanation is also shown in our paper (specifically, the footnote on Page 2).
## Methodology
16. **You'll need to spend a lot more time on figure 2. It is not self-contained at all. You are introducing notation in the figure before you've introduced in the paper. What does each dashed box mean? What are the layers on the top? Why are there arrows? What do the arrows mean? You say you share DAG ok, but then the first box has a matrix which is different from the other two.**  
    Thank you for this suggestion. Before responding to your comments, we would like to quickly review our formulations of the learning objective. According to our ANM assumption, $X_i := f_i(X_{pa_i}) + \epsilon_i, i=1,2,\cdots,d$, where $\epsilon_i$ is mutual independent with any $\epsilon_j$ for $i\neq j$. Then, we have $\epsilon_i = X_i - f_i(X_{pa_i})$. Our learning objective is to maximize the likelihood of joint distribution of noise terms, which is equal to maximize $\prod_{i=1}^{d}p(\epsilon_i)$. Let $\hat{X_i} = f_i(X_{pa_i})$. In our method, we use $h_i(B_{:,i} \circ X)$ to approximate $\hat{X_i}$, where $B$, parameterized by a continuous proxy of adjacency matrix, is the CGL part and $h_i(\cdot)$ is the CMA part. $h_i(\cdot)$ is learned by a neural network. 
    - ***You are introducing notation in the figure before you've introduced in the paper.***  
    We have re-written the caption of Figure 2 to make it informative and self-contained. Notations are well introduced in the caption.
    - ***What does each dashed box mean?***  
    Each grey-dashed box boxed models and data of each client, which means that the local model is updated by learning from local data. While the blue-dashed box boxed all CGLs, which means that this information can be shared among clients and the server.  
    - ***What are the layers on the top?***  
    Since $h_{i}, i=1,2,\cdots,d$ is modeled by neural network, we use three layers to represent neural networks. (This would be replaced and updated in our revision to make it obvious)  
    - ***Why are there arrows? What do the arrows mean?***  
    (1) The whole figure in each gray-dashed box describes $\hat{X} = \prod_{i=1}^{d} h_i(B_{:,i} \circ X)$. Therefore, these directed arrows just describe the procedures from $X$ to $\hat{X}$. (2) the arrow from $U^{c_k}$ to the adjacency matrix means transform $U^{c_k}$ to $B^{c_k}$ by the Gumbel-Sigmoid function. (3) The bidirectional arrows between $U^{c_k}$ and the server means the communication between the server and clients.  
    - ***You say you share DAG ok, but then the first box has a matrix which is different from the other two.***  
    During FCD, all causal graphs (CGs) are not the same at every second. Each client updates its models using its local data for several steps ($it_{fl}$ steps exactly). And then, all $U$s are sent to the server to be averaged. Therefore, in our figure, we want to say that the CGs of some clients may be mislearned. The averaging operation can use CGs of other clients to refine these mislearned ones. Finally, all CGs can converge to one causal graph.

8. **How reasonable is your first assumption? That seems like a very big ask of the data and not mild at all. SEMs and the DAG usually go hand in hand, perhaps the noise model may change a bit between datasets but not the mechanisms themselves (but again, examples would be very welcome).**  
   Sharp idea! Your sense is really good for challenging this assumption from "SEMs and the DAG usually go hand in hand." However, if you read this assumption under the application of FCD, this assumption is definitely acceptable. Firstly, let us skip the IID setting of FCD, which assumes all SEMs are totally the same but data are generated at different local clients. Then, we mainly talk about the Non-IID setting that assumes SEMs vary but DAG is shared among different clients.   
   - Let us follow your line of ***(1)SEMs and the DAG usually go hand in hand, (2)perhaps the noise model may change a bit between datasets but not the mechanisms themselves (but again, examples would be very welcome).***  
   Essentially, a SEM models the physical processes of a system and the generation process behind observations. (1) Intuitively, different SEMs usually describe different systems. Then, naturally, the DAGs may be different. Following this logic, we would say yes that the invariant DAG assumptions among different SEMs are too strong. (2) The assumption that domain shifts can come from the distribution shifts of the exogenous variables (noise terms in our paper) has been widely accepted, such as IP [12] and IRM [13]. So there is no need to argue this one.  
   - Then, let us come back to our FCD. We argue that "different SEMs" is a weak necessary condition of "different systems" but not a sufficient condition. Because a system can have various SEMs at different statuses [14]. Here, we name this kind of system an unstable system. While in the Non-IID setting of FCD, we assume that all clients share an unstable system.  
     - The first example can be fMRI recordings. As pointed in [14], fMRI recordings are usually nonstationary because information flows in the brain may change with stimuli, tasks and attention of the subject. Our federated setting only has one more assumption that fMRI recordings among different clients cannot be shared.  
     - The second example can be causal gene regulatory network inference [16]. The causal direction among genes, i.e., which gene regulates which gene, is believed to be the same. However, in each individual, the SEM mechanism could vary due to individual properties, such as age, gender, etc.  

9.  **Isn't the, what you call "CGL" (I think you mean the learned graph), part very revealing w.r.t. privacy? You may not have access to each individual but instead you are providing organisations with causal information as to how a group of people causally act. In the wrong hands that could be very dangerous. Please comment.**  
    In the federated learning procedures, the server and some clients participate in this process. While as we talked about above, the DAG is shared among all clients. The FCD is motivated by "data on each client is not enough for identifying up the ground-truth DAG". That is to say, the causal graph information is not private for clients. For the server, it depends. In our previous motivations, we actually only care about the "raw data leakage" problem but did not take the privacy of the causal graph into consideration.  
    - In real-world scenarios, some of the causal relations can be public such as diseases research. For these cases, our method can still work. 
    - However, as you suggest, causal graph information sometimes may also be private information. This problem can also be easily solved. In FCD, the only rule of the server is to (1) aggregate and average the CGLs (2) broadcast the new CGL to clients for updating their local CGLs. Therefore, the server can be easily replaced by selecting a client to do the same thing. We name this client as the proxy server. For the proxy server, it needs to play two roles, including training its own model and taking the server's duties. Then, in the communication round, other clients communicate with the proxy server instead of a real server.  

    We will update this discussion in the revision.  
## Preliminaries
10. **You ought to reference Pearl's Causality (2000) and specifically page 203 which defines structural causal models and the associated causal graphical model (which you for some reason decide to call a graphical causal model which is not standard).**  
    We will change our expression to ensure that it is consistent with the definition of Causality book.

content.title: Response to Reviewer FQuA [1/6]
content.comment:
Sincerely, we are grateful to have you, definitely an expert in causality, as our reviewer for evaluating our manuscript and giving many constructive comments. Causal discovery from decentralized data while preventing "raw data leakage" is a totally novel task. So, happy to receive your considerations on our motivations, assumptions, and technique details.    
Before our responses, we prefer to quickly reclaim the motivations of federated causal discovery (FCD).  
- The first strong motivation is the *finite sample problem* for causal discovery. If each client owns enough data to identify the ground truth causal graph, there is no need to perform FCD.    
- To alleviate the above issue, a straightforward solution is to cooperate with other clients whose data are generated according to the same DAG (maybe different SEMs). Here, the *privacy leakage problem* arises since the "raw data" is forbidden to be shared in some situations.   

Your detailed questions are responded point by point as follows and some of them will be updated in our revision to improve the quality of our paper.
## Abstract
1. **You claim "However, data owners gradually refuse to share personalized data to avoid privacy leakage, making this task more troublesome by cutting off the first step" - is this really true? I have not heard this before and it seems data is becoming easier and easier to access as it becomes the norm, certainly within research, to open-source data. Hence, can you point to some sources? I find one in the body of your paper. It seems to be a rather weak case for developing a whole new method.**    
   We get that your consideration is mainly on our motivation of "privacy leakage". With data boosting, it seems that, intuitively, we can easily collect data from multiple sources. We totally agree that your intuition is definitely right in many situations. While, in many other cases, it turns out that the reverse is more practical. Directly, we provide you with two detailed scenes where FCD is highly potential to play its role.  
   - The first example can come from medical scenarios. Exploring causal relations from healthcare data can help to understand the disease mechanisms and causes [2]. However, in real medical scenarios, the diagnostic data of patients are extremely sensitive and absolutely related to personal privacy, which faces very strict data protection regulations, such as HIPAA regulations [8,9]. For some rare diseases, each hospital may own finite clinical data, which, however, is not enough for CD. How can hospitals cooperate to analyze the pathology while preventing sharing patients' privacy (raw diagnostic data)? Naturally, this challenge can be addressed by our method. Depending on how each hospital collects the data, e.g., medical devices, survey design, the data in each hospital may or may not have the same distribution.  
   - The second example can come from the recommendation system (RS) [3,4]. Introducing causal model into RS is becoming prevail since leveraging causality can perform robust recommendation by de-confounding some spurious relations. As users pay more attention to privacy and governments also exacerbate many strict regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [15], which bring increasing difficulties to collect the personal raw data to the server. This is indeed good news for users but a definite disaster for many companies. Accordingly, we think that RS can also benefit from our method. 

## Introduction
2. **Typo: "randomized controlled trials" -> randomized control trials**  
   Both "randomized controlled trials" and "randomized control trials" are fine. We have changed it to "randomized controlled (control) trials" in our revision.
3. **Isn't CSL simply CD i.e. causal discovery?**  
   Yes. We have changed "Causal Structural Learning (CSL)" to "Causal Discovery (CD)" for unified representation.
4. **Typo: "owning to the issue of" -> owing to the issue of**  
   Thanks. This typo is fixed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper develops a DAG structure learning method from decentralized data. The learning is formulated as a continuous optimization problem with an equality acyclicity constraint and solved by gradient descent. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets have been conducted to demonstrate the performance.
content.main_review:
Causal discovery from decentralized and private data is certainly an interesting area. However, the overall contribution of this work is quite marginal. Each local machines learns a DAG model and then the central sever averages them and sends the information back. Such distributed and then combine idea has appeared in previous work, such as:

[1] Danks, D.; Glymour, C.; and Tillman, R. E. Integrating locally learned causal structures with overlapping variables. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS), 2009. 

[2] Tillman, R., and Spirtes, P. Learning equivalence classes of acyclic models with latent and selection variables from multiple datasets with overlapping variables. In Proceedings of the Fourteenth International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), 2011. 

[3] Triantafillou, S., and Tsamardinos, I.. Constraintbased causal discovery from multiple interventions over overlapping variable sets. In Journal of Machine Learning Research, volume 16, 2147–2205, 2015. 

None of the above papers are cited. At a conceptual level, the authors’ approach seems to be quite similar, except the use of the equality acyclicity constraint, a straightforward application of a recent method.

The sever update part (page 5) does not enforce acyclicity constraint. The method takes a random subset of U from the local machines and then take an average. Then the new U may not satisfy the acyclicity constraint in Eq (6). There is no discussion on this issue.

The numerical results are also quite limited:

(a) The synthetic data were simulated from a very sparse setting, d nodes and 2d expected edges. What happens if the DAG is denser?

(b) When the competing methods were applied on separated data, did you try to combine their estimated graphs into an overall estimate?

(c) Some results are a little confused. E.g. Table 1, PC (and a few other competing methods) showed almost identical (or even worse) performance on all data compared to separated data. 

The real data is too small to be useful, only 6 nodes and 7 edges.

From your comments, we find that your considerations are mainly on three aspects: (1) the novelty of our proposed method over some previous works; (2) $U$ may not satisfy the acyclicity constraint, and (3) some considerations on the numerical results. In the following, we will respond to your concerns point by point.  
1. **Causal discovery from decentralized and private data is certainly an interesting area. However, the overall contribution of this work is quite marginal. Each local machine learns a DAG model and then the central sever averages them and sends the information back. Such distributed and then combine idea has appeared in previous work, such as [1], [2] and [3]. None of the above papers are cited. At a conceptual level, the authors’ approach seems to be quite similar, except the use of the equality acyclicity constraint, a straightforward application of a recent method.**  
   Thanks for providing these papers missed by us! Fortunately, we find that the problem considered in our paper is *considerably different* from these references after carefully reading them. The main differences are as follows:  
   - These references are handling another important topic named *Overlapping datasets problem* [1,2,3,5] in the causal discovery (CD) field or *Graph quilting* [4] in the undirected graph learning field. They also consider multiple datasets but assume that *non-identical variables in different datasets but may be overlapped*. Their task mainly lies in how to learn *the full DAG* from multiple datasets. Their technique challenge is mainly on how to combine *sub-graphs* learned from different datasets into an *integrated graph*. In these works, data from different sites need to be put together on a central server. 
   - Our motivation comes from assuming that *data on each local client can not well identify up the ground truth causal graph because of finite sample problem*. Furthermore, to avoid data leakage, the local data must be stored on the local client and not shared between clients and the server. 
   - Considering the technique lines, our method is also different from these papers. Our method formulates the overall learning task by a continuous optimization problem, which can be easily solved by gradient descent methods. To my knowledge, in the research field of *Overlapping datasets problem*, there is no such similar formulation.  

   Therefore, these two lines of methods seem similar but totally with different settings, different motivations and different technical lines, of course. Considering your suggestion *"none of the above papers are cited"*, we will update these differences in our related work part. Please let me know if you have any further doubt about this explanation.

12. **The theorems do not relate to the proposed method in any way. I believe simply citing the existing identifiability results would be sufficient. It might be misleading to have a proposition that has nothing to do with federated learning.**  
   Agreed that the theorem does not relate to the proposed method. However, we think that identifiability conditions of CD are for the data generation models such as LiNGAM, ANM, and PNL rather than a specific method.  
   Also, we agree with you that no novel condition is proposed. However, learning DAG from decentralized data is still a new setting. The new thing is that even some clients only have data distributions that can only be identified up to the Markov Equivalence Class (MEC), they can be leveraged to jointly learn the ground-truth DAG (at least DAGs share the same skeleton with the ground-truth DAG). For this reason, we decide to keep this theorem.  
   Considering your suggestion, we also worry about misleading things. Therefore, we decide to move this part to the Appendix.  
13. **Could you please explain how the proposed method is outperforming, for example, GES or NOTEARS with all data brought together in the IID setting? I am not sure how to explain this.**  
   Good question. We need to clarify that this credit belongs to MCSL but not our method.  
      - First of all, PC and GES can only reach the CPDAG (or MEC) at most, which shares the same Skelton with the ground-truth DAG. When we evaluate SHD, we just ignore the direction of undirected edges learned by PC and GES. That is to say, these two methods can get SHD $0$ if they can identify the CPDAG. Therefore, the final results are not caused by unfair comparison.
      - For PC, the independence test is leveraged to decode the (conditional) independence from the data distribution. Therefore, the accuracy would be affected by (1) the amount of the observations and (2) the effectiveness of "the non-parametric kernel independence test" method. 
      - GES leverages greedy search with BIC score. However, the likelihood part of BIC in GES is Linear Gaussian, which is unsuitable for data generated by the Non-linear model.
      - NOTEARS is a linear model but the causal mechanisms are non-linear. The reason will be the unfitness between data and model.  
      - DAG-GNN is also a non-linear model. However, the non-linear assumption of DAG-GNN is not the same as the data generation model assumed in our paper. The second reason comes from its "mechanisms approximation" (forgive us for still using this term) modules are compulsory to share some parameters.  
      - Both NOTEARS-MLP and MCSL have their own advantages. Please refer to Tables 7 and 8 in the Appendix, you will find that NOTEARS-MLP performs better when the non-linear functions are MIM and MLP while MCSL works better on GP and GP-add models.  
      
      Finishing the above discussions of other methods, let us come back to discuss *Why our method is outperforming* even some baseline methods using all data for training. 
      - Let us first discuss the AS-FCD (All-Shared FCD), which shares all model parameters (both $\Phi$ and $U$) among all clients. If we set $it_{fl}$ as $1$ in AS-FCD, AS-FCD is totally the same as MCSL using all data for training. For simplicity, we mark all parameters (actually $\Phi$ and $U$) of client $c_k$ together as $\theta^{c_k}$. Let us consider the $t$-th iteration when all clients receive the average parameters $\theta_t$ from the server and update their parameters by $\theta_t$.  
         - For AS-FCD, firstly, we mark the gradients obtained by using the local data of client  $c^k$ for $k \in \[m\]$ as $g^\{c_k\}_t$. Then each client $c_k$ updates its parameters for one step by $ \theta^\{c_k\}_t = \theta_t - lr \times g^\{c_k\}_t $, where $lr$ is the learning rate. Afterwards, the server collects all parameters and averages them to get $\theta_\{t+1\}= \frac{\sum_\{k=1\}^m (\theta_t - lr \times g_t^{c_k})}{m} =\theta_t-lr \times \frac{\sum_\{k=1\}^{m} g^{c_k}_t}{m}$.
         - For MCSL, there is only one $\theta$. If MCSL uses full gradient information, then $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t-lr \times \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{m} g^{c_k}_t}{m}$ (the full gradient is just the average of gradients from all samples).  
         
         We can find that the updated parameters are totally the same. Then if $it_{fl} > 1$, we average all parameters every $it_{fl}$ iterations. Even though the exact updating procedures are not the same, the expectations of updated parameters are the same. This is why we say that *MCSL trained on all data can serve as an approximate upper bound of our method but unobtainable.* in our paper. 
      
      - In DS-FCD (DAG-Shared FCD) method, only all causal graphs are averaged. However, this partial information-sharing mechanism also helps on benefiting information from other clients to find a better solution [6].

Firstly, discovering the ground-truth DAG is an NP-hard problem. Traditional methods like PC and GES search the discrete DAG space to solve this problem, which are relatively time-consuming. Then, NOTEARS introduces an equality constraint (${\rm Tr}[e^{B}] - d = 0$) to formulate the DAG search problem as a continuous optimization problem, which can be easily solved by the gradient descent methods. content.title: Response to Reviewer tbd8 [1/5]
content.comment:
Sincerely, feel grateful and happy to have you as the reviewer of our paper. Your valuable feedback inspires us a lot to rethink the clearness of our expressions in the paper. Before our responses, we would like to quickly review the motivations of federated causal discovery (FCD).  
- The first strong motivation is the *finite sample problem* for causal discovery. If each client owns enough data to identify the ground truth causal graph, there is no need to implement FCD.   
- To alleviate the above issue, a straightforward solution is to cooperate with other clients whose data are generated according to the same DAG (maybe different SEMs). Here, the *privacy leakage problem* arises since the "raw data" is forbidden to be shared in some situations.  

In the following, we will respond to your concerns point by point and some of them will be updated in our revision to improve the quality of our paper.   
1. **I believe the setup needs a bit more justification. Could you give real-world examples where federated causal structure learning is needed?**  
   Because compared to traditional CD, the IID setting of FCD just brings one more assumption that local data cannot be directly collected owing to the consideration of "privacy leakage". Non-IID setting further relaxes the assumption to data heterogeneity case, where causal mechanisms may also vary among different local data distributions. Therefore, our method could be directly applied to the applications of CD *where privacy is also very important*.  
   - The first example can come from medical science. Exploring causal relations from healthcare data can help to understand the disease mechanisms and causes [2]. However, in real medical scenarios, the clinical data of patients are extremely sensitive and absolutely related to personal privacy, which faces very strict data protection regulations, such as HIPAA regulations [1]. For some rare diseases, each hospital may own finite clinical data, which, however, is not enough for CD. How can hospitals cooperate to analyze the pathology while preventing sharing patients' privacy (raw diagnostic data)? Naturally, this challenge can be addressed by our method. Depending on how each hospital collects the data, e.g., medical devices, survey design, the data in each hospital may or may not have the same distribution.  
   - The second example can come from the recommendation system (RS) [3,4]. Introducing causal model into RS is becoming prevail since leveraging causality can perform robust recommendation by de-confounding some spurious relations. As users pay more attention to privacy and governments also exacerbate many strict regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [8], which bring increasing difficulties to collect the personal raw data to the server. This is indeed good news for users but a definite disaster for many companies. Accordingly, we think that RS can also benefit from our method.  
   
   Based on the aforementioned examples, we argue that FCD will earn its value and be paid high attention. 
2. **The "shift concept" mentioned in passing in the introduction should be explained in a bit more detail to convey the point more clearly.**  
   Thanks for the nice suggestion. Concepts of "label shift" and "covariate shift" are frequently appeared in the domain adaptation/generalization field but may be unfamiliar to others. Therefore, we changed our expressions as *"FL usually cares about classification tasks where data heterogeneity is assumed by some specific distribution shift types such as label shift (the shift of $P(Y)$) or covariate shift (the shift of $P(X)$), while FCD handles a generative model where data heterogeneity means the joint distribution shift of all variables, which would bring more challenges compared to the model design in the FL paradigm."*
3. **Mechanism approximation is not typically used in non-parametric causal discovery. Please explain in the introduction why this approach is taken. [turns out this is due to ANM assumption but it should be mentioned early on]**  
   Agreed. In traditional non-parametric CD, constraint-based methods are often used to find the DAG by leveraging the (conditional) independence relationships encoded in the data distribution. If the causal relations (mechanisms) are non-linear between the variable and its parents, a prevailing way for testing the (conditional) independence may lie in designing the "Kernel Conditional Independence Test" methods.   
   Our method follows the other research line of score-based methods, where the non-parametric part of the model is often used to directly model the non-linear causal relations (mechanisms) between each variable and its parents, such as NOTEARS, NOTEARS-MLP and GranDAG. Therefore, "Mechanism approximation" is often used although it is not well known in causality. We prefer to keep it in our paper and mention it early according to your suggestion.

content.title: Response to your "After Rebuttal"
content.comment:
Feel excited to receive your response and happy to see that there is no other doubt other than the experimental results. Because the rebuttal phase is not closed yet, we sincerely hope to receive your "detailed doubt". In the following, we would like to reclarify why our method seems ***"too good to be true"***.  

***"federation" does not cause too much loss in the power of the causal discovery tests.***  
   Yes. Compared to the baseline method, "Federation" does not cause too much loss if the data is IID. If the communication frequency $it_{fl}=1$, our AS-FCD is the same as the baseline method MCSL, not to mention the "loss" thing since there is no "loss". We believe that we have thoroughly explained this before.   

***Currently it seems like it outperforms everything including the centralized methods which seems too good to be true and indicates that the message of the paper is quite confusing.***

According to your kind suggestion, we have added the setting of linear data in our Appendix to make the comparison fairly. Then, we thoroughly discuss the linear and non-linear cases, respectively. Your concern is mainly on that why our method can outperform other methods even they use all data. 
- Non-Linear Case.  
  For this case, the compared methods are PC, NOTEARS-MLP, DAG-GNN, and MCSL. Our FCD is developed highly based on MCSL.  
  (1) MCSL can outperform PC and DAG-GNN.  
  (2) MCSL performs better than NOTEARS-MLP if the non-linear function is GP, MIM, and GP-add. NOTEARS-MLP outperforms MCSL if the non-linear function is MLP.   
  (3) In the IID case, our AS-FCD is equal to MCSL if $it_{fl} = 1$ (the communication step). If $it_{fl} > 1$, the expectated gradients of AS-FCD and MCSL are equal. DS-FCD will show worse results than MCSL and AS-FCD since less information is shared among clients. Therefore, we call MCSL the *approximate upper bound* of our method.  
  Based on the above conclusions, please refer to Tables 1, 14, and 15. You will find  
  (1) **MCSL with all data always shows better results than our AS-FCD and DS-FCD.**  
  (2) If the function is MLP, NOTEARS-MLP shows better results than MCSL and our methods, of course.  
  (3) In other cases, our results can approximate the results of MCSL. Therefore, it is not weird that our methods are better than other baseline methods.  
  (4) We have explained that the credit belongs to MCSL rather than our methods in our paper. Hope that the authors of MCSL can hear the admiration.

- Linear Case.  
   The baseline methods are NOTEARS and GES. There is no fair/unfair concern on this since they both are designed for linear gaussian data.  
   (1) NOTEARS is better than GES owing to the advantage of "continuous search" over "greedy search".  
   (2) Our AS-FCD is based on NOTEARS so that our method can approximate the results of NOTEARS.  
   Based on the above conclusions, please refer to Table 7. You will find  
   (1) **NOTEARS with all data performs mostly better than our method.**  
   (2) Our method can approximate the results of NOTEARS. Therefore, it is not weird that our method is better than GES.  
   (3) We have explained that the credit belongs to NOTEARS rather than our method in our paper. Hope that the authors of NOTEARS can hear the admiration.

In conclusion, here, we think that "too good" is a positive comment. But, the credits belong to our baseline methods MCSL and NOTEARS. Our results are not better than MCSL and NOTEARS.  
We appreciate your efforts in helping us improve our paper. Considering your doubt on the experimental results, we indeed think that (1) our experimental results are reasonable (2) and our explanations are clear.  
Would you mind directly pointing out which part of our results is still confusing?
